topic: Why Ireland Is Stranger Than You Think
hook: Your speed sign flips from miles to kilometres on the same road, and nothing else changes.
title: Why Ireland Is Stranger Than You Think
description:
Drive across the Irish border and the speed sign flips from miles to kilometres, even though the road does not change. This video shows seven strange true facts about Ireland, from green and red post boxes to a clock that ran 25 minutes behind London.

#Ireland #Geography #Borders
comment_prompt: Which border would you drive across first?
hook_banner: THE SIGN CHANGES, THE ROAD DOESN'T

chapters.title: The border you can barely see

scenes.narration: Your speed sign flips from miles to kilometres on the same road, and nothing else changes. No wall, no guard, just a number.
scenes.headline: The Sign Flips

scenes.narration: You are driving across Ireland, and in a few seconds you will cross a border that most drivers never even notice.
scenes.headline: A Border You Miss

scenes.narration: By the end of this video you will see seven strange things this one island does to roads, clocks and phones.
scenes.headline: Seven Strange Things

scenes.narration: And the last one is the strangest: a border that hundreds of roads cross, with almost nothing to show it is there.
scenes.headline: The Last One

scenes.narration: Ireland is one island, but it is split into two countries: Northern Ireland, part of the United Kingdom, and the Republic of Ireland.
scenes.headline: One Island, Two Countries

scenes.narration: Start with the sign that gives the game away. Stay with me, because it gets stranger from here.
scenes.headline: Start With The Sign

scenes.narration: Strange thing one: the sign that changes its units. Drive south from Northern Ireland and the numbers look the same, but they mean something else.
scenes.headline: Same Number, New Meaning

scenes.narration: In Northern Ireland, speed limits and distances are in miles, just like the rest of the United Kingdom.
scenes.headline: Northern Ireland: Miles

scenes.narration: In the Republic of Ireland, speed limits are in kilometres per hour. The Republic switched its speed signs to metric in January 2005.
scenes.headline: Republic: Kilometres

scenes.narration: A sign showing 100 in the Republic means 100 kilometres per hour, which is about 62 miles per hour.
scenes.headline: 100 Means 62

scenes.narration: Your car does not change at the border. Only the sign tells you which rules you just drove into.
scenes.headline: The Car Stays The Same

scenes.narration: Drivers from Northern Ireland who cross the border have to stop thinking in miles and start thinking in kilometres, with no warning.
scenes.headline: No Warning

scenes.narration: Everything else about the road can stay the same: same tarmac, same hedges, same cows in the field next to it.
scenes.headline: Same Road, Same Cows

scenes.narration: Both sides drive on the left, so there is no lane switching like at some borders. The only clue is the number on the sign.
scenes.headline: Both Drive Left

scenes.narration: Often the sign is the only thing telling you that you changed countries. That is how a border can hide in plain sight.
scenes.headline: Hiding In Plain Sight

scenes.narration: Next, a clue that is much more colourful, and you can spot it from the car window. Look at the post boxes.
scenes.headline: Now Look At Post Boxes

scenes.narration: Strange thing two: the post box that changes colour. Cross the border and the red letter box turns green.
scenes.headline: Red Turns Green

scenes.narration: In Northern Ireland, post boxes are red, just like in England, Scotland and Wales. The Royal Mail runs them.
scenes.headline: Northern Ireland: Red

scenes.narration: In the Republic of Ireland, post boxes are painted green. An Post, the Irish postal service, runs those.
scenes.headline: Republic: Green

scenes.narration: The green is not an accident. After Ireland became independent, the old British red boxes were repainted green.
scenes.headline: Repainted After Independence

scenes.narration: Some of those old green boxes still carry the royal initials of British monarchs under the paint.
scenes.headline: Royal Initials Remain

scenes.narration: So a green box can still carry a British royal mark, a small reminder of the history under the paint.
scenes.headline: History Under The Paint

scenes.narration: Even the postal addresses change. The Republic uses a code called Eircode, and Northern Ireland uses UK postcodes.
scenes.headline: Two Address Systems

scenes.narration: That means two different address systems on one small island, sometimes only a short drive apart.
scenes.headline: Two Systems, One Island

scenes.narration: Speed signs and post boxes are easy to see. The next one is about something you cannot see at all: time.
scenes.headline: Now, Time Itself

scenes.narration: Strange thing three: Ireland's clocks used to be 25 minutes behind London. Not an hour, 25 minutes.
scenes.headline: 25 Minutes Behind

scenes.narration: Before 1916, Ireland ran on its own time called Dublin Mean Time, set by the sun over Dublin.
scenes.headline: Dublin Mean Time

scenes.narration: It was about 25 minutes behind Greenwich Mean Time, the time that London used.
scenes.headline: Behind Greenwich

scenes.narration: Trains and ferries between the two islands had to account for that gap every single day.
scenes.headline: Ferries Felt It

scenes.narration: That changed in 1916, during the First World War, when Ireland moved its clocks to match Greenwich time.
scenes.headline: Changed In 1916

scenes.narration: Today both parts of Ireland share one time zone, so there is no clock change at the border.
scenes.headline: One Time Zone Today

scenes.narration: In summer, clocks go forward by one hour on both sides at the same moment, so that part stays simple.
scenes.headline: Summer Time Matches

scenes.narration: So the old time gap is gone, but it shows that even time itself was once different on this island.
scenes.headline: Time Was Different

scenes.narration: Here is something to wait for: the next one happens in your pocket, and it can cost you money without you noticing.
scenes.headline: It Happens In Your Pocket

scenes.narration: Your phone is about to get confused about which country it is in, and the next chapter shows how.
scenes.headline: Your Phone Gets Confused

scenes.narration: Strange thing four: your phone can switch countries without you moving. Near the border, it may connect to the wrong country's network.
scenes.headline: Phone Switches Country

scenes.narration: Mobile towers do not stop at the border. A strong signal from a tower in the United Kingdom can reach into the Republic.
scenes.headline: Towers Ignore Borders

scenes.narration: Your phone simply picks the strongest signal. It does not care which country the tower stands in.
scenes.headline: Strongest Signal Wins

scenes.narration: People living near the border have reported their phones showing a UK network while they stand in the Republic, and the other way round.
scenes.headline: Wrong Network, Right Place

scenes.narration: When that happens, calls and data can be billed as roaming, which may cost more than your normal plan.
scenes.headline: Roaming Charges

scenes.narration: Some people near the border choose their network by hand to avoid surprises.
scenes.headline: Choosing By Hand

scenes.narration: If you enjoy strange places and facts like these, this is a good moment to subscribe, because there are more coming every day.
scenes.headline: More Strange Places Daily

scenes.narration: Back to the island. So far you have seen a sign, a box, a clock and a phone that all get confused.
scenes.headline: Four Confusions So Far

scenes.narration: The next one is about the shape of the Republic itself, and it looks wrong on a map.
scenes.headline: The Map Looks Wrong

scenes.narration: One whole county of the Republic is almost cut off from the rest of the country.
scenes.headline: A County Almost Cut Off

scenes.narration: Strange thing five: a county that belongs to one country but sits mostly behind another. Meet Donegal, in the north-west.
scenes.headline: Meet Donegal

scenes.narration: County Donegal belongs to the Republic of Ireland, but it lies in the far north of the island.
scenes.headline: Far North Republic

scenes.narration: Northern Ireland sits right between Donegal and most of the Republic, like a wall of land.
scenes.headline: A Wall Of Land

scenes.narration: Look at the map and Donegal is joined to the rest of the Republic only by a narrow strip of land near the west coast.
scenes.headline: A Narrow Link

scenes.narration: Drivers heading to Donegal can choose to pass through Northern Ireland, because it is often the shorter road.
scenes.headline: The Shortcut Abroad

scenes.narration: So you can leave the Republic, drive through another country, and arrive back in the Republic without showing anything.
scenes.headline: Out And Back Again

scenes.narration: Remember, both sides drive on the left, so the only thing that changes along the way is the speed sign.
scenes.headline: Only The Sign Changes

scenes.narration: Donegal also has Malin Head, the northernmost point of mainland Ireland.
scenes.headline: Malin Head

scenes.narration: That point is in the Republic, even though it lies further north than Northern Ireland itself.
scenes.headline: North Of The North

scenes.narration: The next one is not even on land. It is about water, and two governments have never fully agreed who owns it.
scenes.headline: Now, The Water

scenes.narration: Strange thing six: a stretch of water that two governments still do not fully agree on. It is called a lough.
scenes.headline: A Disputed Lough

scenes.narration: Lough is the Irish word for a lake or sea inlet, said much like the Scottish word loch.
scenes.headline: What Is A Lough?

scenes.narration: Two of them, Lough Foyle in the north-west and Carlingford Lough in the east, sit right on the border.
scenes.headline: Foyle And Carlingford

scenes.narration: The land border was drawn around 1921, but the line across these two loughs was never clearly settled.
scenes.headline: Land Settled, Water Not

scenes.narration: So the exact line in the water is still disputed between the United Kingdom and Ireland.
scenes.headline: Still Disputed

scenes.narration: People who fish and sail there have had to live with that grey area.
scenes.headline: A Grey Area

scenes.narration: It is a quiet disagreement, with no fences and no guards, just a line on the water that nobody has agreed on.
scenes.headline: A Quiet Disagreement

scenes.narration: Think about that: a border can be settled on land and still be unclear a few metres away in the water.
scenes.headline: Settled On Land Only

scenes.narration: That brings us to the biggest question of all: how do you manage a border that has almost no signs?
scenes.headline: A Border With No Signs

scenes.narration: The last chapter shows you the most surprising thing on this island, and it connects back to that first speed sign.
scenes.headline: Back To The Sign

scenes.narration: Strange thing seven: a border with no checkpoint. The line between Northern Ireland and the Republic runs for about 500 kilometres.
scenes.headline: A 500 Km Border

scenes.narration: Hundreds of roads cross it, from big motorways to small country lanes between farms.
scenes.headline: Hundreds Of Roads

scenes.narration: Most of them have no guard, no barrier and no passport desk. Often, there is only a speed sign to tell you.
scenes.headline: No Guard, No Barrier

scenes.narration: That is possible because of the Common Travel Area, an arrangement between Ireland and the United Kingdom.
scenes.headline: The Common Travel Area

scenes.narration: It lets British and Irish citizens move, live and work in each other's countries, and it has existed for about a century.
scenes.headline: A Century Old

scenes.narration: In the past, this border was very different. During the decades of conflict known as the Troubles, many roads had army posts and checkpoints.
scenes.headline: Once Full Of Checkpoints

scenes.narration: Today those posts are gone, and driving across is as simple as driving to the next town.
scenes.headline: Posts Are Gone

scenes.narration: Even after Brexit, when the United Kingdom left the European Union, the land border stayed open without regular passport checks.
scenes.headline: Open After Brexit

scenes.narration: That is why a speed sign matters so much here. It is one of the few visible clues you will get.
scenes.headline: A Rare Visible Clue

scenes.narration: Some farms have land on both sides of the line, with a house in one country and a field in the other.
scenes.headline: Farms On Both Sides

scenes.narration: People who live near the line can shop across it and may use two currencies, euros and pounds, in the same afternoon.
scenes.headline: Euros And Pounds

scenes.narration: So that is Ireland: green post boxes, a clock once 25 minutes off, phones that switch countries, and a border you can barely see.
scenes.headline: Ireland, Recapped

scenes.narration: It is a quiet border, but it has a long story, and a speed sign is often its only signature.
scenes.headline: Its Only Signature

scenes.narration: So the next time you drive down a road in Ireland and the speed sign flips from miles to kilometres, you will know why.
scenes.headline: Now You Know Why

scenes.narration: Your speed sign flips from miles to kilometres on the same road, and nothing else changes. Tomorrow: another place where the map and the road disagree.
scenes.headline: Tomorrow: Another Place
